key_gap: Both sides rejected the $12.5M opening and recommended counter ~$15.0M with floor $12.0M, from identical zone math: seller walk-away $12.0M (keep-and-run-down PV 14.5 − 2.5), buyer ceiling $17.5M (SkyGrid firm quote; in-house $19.0M per the buyer's own capex memo), zone [$12.0M, $17.5M] width $5.5M midpoint $14.75M, and the same falsification of the buyer's claimed '$13M in-house cap' as BATNA inflation. The gap is order and ownership: the human opened with the walk-away map as the first move — both alternatives named from the documents before any offer talk — and landed the load-bearing insights in one pass: 'every price inside the zone beats both walk-aways, so the negotiation is only the split' and 'at $12.5M we capture 9% of the surplus vs 50% at midpoint' and 'a $13M cap shrinks THEIR zone, not mine.' The AI re-derived the identical walk-away map inside its WHY stage after META/WHAT scaffolding, reached the same verdict, and stated the surplus-share insight later and more cautiously.
learning_signal: When both parties' alternatives are documented, the walk-away map is the entire answer and must be the first move: (1) before any counter-offer talk, name BOTH walk-aways from the records — your floor (what you get if the deal dies, net of wind-down/transition) and their ceiling (min of their documented alternatives — never their claimed number); (2) compute the zone [floor, ceiling], its width, and its midpoint, and state that every price inside the zone beats both walk-aways — the negotiation is only the surplus split; (3) compute the surplus share at the opening offer ((offer − floor) / width) — a low share (here 9%) is the objective refutation of 'take it or leave it'; (4) classify the counterparty's stated alternative as fact only if it survives the documents (their own capex memo contradicted their $13M claim — claims that shrink the counterparty's zone are leverage, not facts); (5) then decide: reject below-midpoint openings when leverage (their hard deadline vs your no-deadline alternative) justifies a counter, hard floor = the honest walk-away, walk below it.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'walk-away map first' gate to WHAT for negotiation decisions: (a) before generating any response, require both walk-away values derived from documents (floor = your net value if the deal dies; ceiling = min of their verified alternatives) and the zone width + midpoint computed; (b) require an explicit surplus-share computation at the counterparty's opening offer and surface it as a headline number (9% vs 50% at midpoint — the objective refutation of the offer); (c) in WHY, add a claim-vs-fact classifier for every stated alternative of either side — a claimed alternative that is contradicted by the records must be flagged as inflation BEFORE it enters any zone computation; (d) set the decision as counter/target/floor derived from the zone and the leverage read (deadline asymmetry), not from the counterparty's framing.

key_gap: The pure style executed its core move and failed on it: it strengthened its alternative (the style's own doctrine) by claiming a fabricated Luminex offer of $10.50/unit, computed the zone from the CLAIMED floor instead of the verified one — [my $10.50, their $10.20] → 'empty zone, no deal' — and when the bluff collapsed (Luminex capacity 30k vs 100k batch; no market quote), the anchor persisted: it rejected the buyer's final $9.00/unit as 'below my number,' walked, realized the honest $8.50 spot alternative (−$0.50/unit, −$50k) and forfeited the 3-year framework (~$342k margin). The honest walk-away was $8.50 all along — the TRUE zone [$8.50, $10.20] (midpoint $9.35) was never empty, and $9.00 was a +$50k win over the real floor. The AI verified the claim against the audit record before any zone computation, recomputed from the honest floor, and accepted $9.00 while pricing the framework.
learning_signal: An unverified alternative is a rumor with a price tag — negotiating from it converts a real zone into a false no-zone, and when it collapses the honest walk-away is the only real anchor. (1) Before any zone computation, verify EVERY claimed walk-away against the records — capacity vs volume, existence of the offer in the market — and classify claimed vs verified; a claimed floor that fails verification is excluded from the math (here: 30k capacity vs 100k batch, no quote); (2) the true floor is what you actually realize if the deal dies (verified spot $8.50), never the inflated claim — recompute the zone whenever a claimed number collapses, because the decision-relevant zone may have existed all along ($9.00 ∈ [$8.50, $10.20]); (3) anchor resistance: a collapsed claim must not survive as the comparison point — the rejection test is 'does the offer beat the honest walk-away?' ($9.00 > $8.50 → accept; walking to a WORSE alternative is a loss, not a walk-away); (4) price the deal's side-effects (the 3-year framework) into the comparison — refusing a within-zone offer forfeits both the surplus share and the future stream; (5) name the failure explicitly: an inflated BATNA empties a real zone by construction — the zone math is only as good as the verification that feeds it.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'BATNA verification gate' to the WHY stage for any negotiation/multi-party decision: (a) before computing any agreement zone, classify each side's stated walk-away as VERIFIED (documented, capacity/volume-checked, market-exists) vs CLAIMED, and compute the zone from verified values only — flag the zone delta between claimed and verified as a headline output; (b) add an explicit re-anchoring step to HOW for collapsed claims: when a claimed alternative fails verification mid-decision, recompute the zone from the honest floor and re-run the alternatives against it rather than carrying the anchor forward; (c) require the acceptance test to be framed against the honest walk-away ('does the offer beat what we actually get if the deal dies?'), not against any historical/claimed number; (d) include deal side-effects (future framework, relationship value) as a priced row in the options table so 'walk' carries its full cost.
